content_html:
CXC and DMC are separate brands even though many CXC threads use numbering intended to correspond with DMC codes. Matching numbers make substitution easier, but they do not turn the two fibers into the same product.

This guide resolves the situation with practical criteria and avoids automatic fixes that can make the project worse or add unnecessary work.

The difference that matters

Material and construction

DMC Mouliné Spécial is 100 percent mercerized cotton. Specialist comparisons commonly describe standard CXC floss as a poly-cotton blend with somewhat different feel, thickness and sheen.

Color, sheen and coverage

Colors are often close, but they should not be assumed identical. Switching brand in the middle of one large block can make a small difference in hue or sheen visible across the surface.

When substitution makes sense

CXC can be attractive for price and for familiar numbering across many shades. Before buying a full palette, test representative colors on the fabric you intend to use.

When mixing is risky

For a new project, using one brand throughout can work well when its palette suits the design. Mixing is less risky for isolated accents than inside gradients or large continuous areas.

How a pattern should state it

Our patterns can use DMC as the design reference and allow substitution, but they should not promise that another brand with matching numbers will create an identical stitched sample.

Overall, the best solution preserves stability, readability and a reasonable stitching experience. Our editorial content should explain why, and our patterns should apply the same judgment to materials, layout and working notes.

CXC and DMC should be treated as different thread products even when a CXC label uses a number intended to correspond with a familiar DMC reference. Numbering can make substitution convenient, but it does not guarantee identical fiber composition, sheen, thickness, dye behavior or color under every light. If a project contains large solid blocks or a subtle gradient, compare the actual skeins before changing brand halfway through.

Coverage is one of the first practical differences to test. Two strands from one brand may spread slightly differently from two strands of another on the same fabric count. Stitch a small square with the same needle, strand count and tension and compare from normal viewing distance. If one thread gives visibly fuller coverage, you may prefer it for dark fabric or reduce strands on a finer count.

Color matching should be evaluated as a family, not only one code at a time. A single substitute can look acceptable in isolation and still disrupt a three-color shadow sequence when its undertone is warmer or cooler than the neighboring threads. Portraits and photographic conversions deserve particular caution because smooth transitions depend on relative differences between several shades.

Mixing brands within one project is possible, but record every substitution. If you later need more thread, a note prevents guessing which brand was used in which area. For a large solid region, avoid switching brand or batch mid-block unless a physical test shows the change is invisible, because differences in sheen can appear even when the hue looks close.

For MAKE, DMC can remain the reference system in our PDFs while customers retain the option to substitute. We should never promise that a matching CXC number will reproduce the sample exactly. A short substitution note can explain that equivalent-number systems are starting points and that physical comparison is recommended for color-critical designs.

Needle feel is worth testing alongside color. A thread that is slightly thicker or softer can change how easily several strands pass through a fine count, and that affects speed and surface texture. Comparing only loose skeins misses part of the real stitching experience.

If a project switches brands intentionally, make the boundary logical. Using one brand for an entire background and another for a separate motif is safer than alternating brands stitch by stitch in one smooth gradient. Consistency within a visual area usually matters more than brand purity across the whole piece.

For future material guides, we can document tested substitutions without calling them exact equivalents. “Tested alternative with a close visual result” is more honest and useful than a conversion table that implies identical fiber and dye.

Wash and care behavior can differ with fiber composition, so if the finished object will be washed frequently, test the substitute under the intended care routine. A color match at the start is not the only criterion for towels, cushions or clothing.

When sharing a substitution in project notes, record brand as well as number. Writing only “310” can be ambiguous later if several brands in the stash use DMC-like numbering. Clear records make repeat projects much easier.
